title: Knowledge Check 6: Lessons 41-48
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 41-48 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: How does building a site on the Lightning Web Runtime differ architecturally from building on Aura?
options: It renders every component dynamically at request time, so a component change shows with no republish.
It pre-compiles and caches its static content at publish time, so a component change needs a republish.
It keeps the component code only inside the org data center, so no content delivery network is ever used at all.
It restores a generic record detail page that can be placed on any page type without a rebuild.
questions.explanation: The runtime assembles the page when you publish, trading instant component changes for cached, pre-compiled delivery.

questions.question: An org offers a public knowledge base that anonymous visitors read and a portal where customers log in to track their own cases. How should external licensing be sized?
options: Every anonymous reader consumes an external license, while logged-in customers consume none.
Both of the audiences share a single site license billed by the number of page views served.
Anonymous readers consume no external license, while each logged-in customer consumes one.
Each logged-in customer is instead given an internal license to keep the portal cost down.
questions.explanation: External licenses attach to users, so a session with no licensed user behind it costs nothing, and a login is what requires the license.

questions.question: How does a sharing set decide which records an external user may see?
options: It keys access to the user's own account or contact relationship and does not roll up the hierarchy.
It grants record access based on the role hierarchy that sits above the user's own external role.
It shares all records with every user who belongs to the same site, regardless of their own account.
It exposes every record of an object because external users always bypass the org-wide defaults.
questions.explanation: A sharing set maps records through the user's account or contact link, and because it does not roll up, superiors gain nothing from it.

questions.question: A child component must notify a grandparent that sits above an intermediate component's shadow boundary. How must its event be configured?
options: With bubbles and composed both true, because each defaults false and the event must cross a shadow root.
With bubbles set to true only, because composed is implied automatically whenever any shadow root exists in the tree.
With composed set to true only, because events bubble upward through the DOM by default in every case.
With neither property set, because events always propagate automatically to every ancestor component.
questions.explanation: Bubbling and shadow-boundary crossing are separate and both default to false, so an event that must reach a grandparent sets both.

questions.question: Under the composition contract for Lightning web components, how does information move between a parent and its children?
options: Data flows up from a child to its parent through public attributes, and errors flow back through events.
Data flows down from parent to child through public attributes, and consequences flow up through events.
Data and the events both flow in only one direction, from the parent component down to each child.
Children read and change their parent's state directly, so no events are needed between the two.
questions.explanation: The one-directional contract passes data down as attributes and sends outcomes back up as events, which keeps each side decoupled.

questions.question: A component saves a record with an imperative call and, on the same screen, shows a wired read of that record. What keeps the wired read from going stale?
options: Nothing is needed, because a wired read re-provisions itself automatically after any write to a record.
Re-import the wire adapter and re-declare the wired property after the write has fully been completed.
Convert the read into a cacheable write so that the framework refreshes both of the data paths together.
Call refreshApex on the wired result once the write resolves, because the cache and the write disagree.
questions.explanation: A wired read shares the client cache with no knowledge of an imperative write, so the write must explicitly refresh the wired result.

questions.question: What does enabling the Salesforce CDN for the Lightning component framework actually deliver?
options: It caches the org's record data and metadata so that records are served from a location nearer the user.
It caches the framework's static script and JSON files for faster loads, not record data or metadata.
It replaces the client-side data cache completely, so that Lightning Data Service is no longer needed.
It is already enabled inside every org, so the setting needs no review during a performance pass.
questions.explanation: The CDN accelerates delivery of the framework files themselves; it never carries your org's records or metadata.

questions.question: A component needs a third-party charting library. Which delivery approach follows performance guidance?
options: Upload it as a static resource with Public cache control and load it once on the render that needs it.
Reference the library from a public internet URL and reload the entire file on every render to stay current.
Hide the chart region with CSS so the library never blocks the page during its initial render pass.
Load the library once per user session from an external host and skip the static resource entirely.
questions.explanation: A cached static resource loaded once on first render keeps the library out of the render path and lets the platform serve it efficiently.

questions.question: Two users open the same Lightning page in the same org and see different experienced page time. What best explains this?
options: Experienced page time is measured entirely on the server, so it cannot vary between any two users.
The org configuration differs for each user, which is the only factor that shapes the load time.
Network conditions and device capability set a floor outside the org's control, so the same page differs.
The difference proves a defect, because the platform is supposed to serve every single user an identical page load.
questions.explanation: Only org configuration is yours to engineer; the network, device, and browser of each user set a floor you cannot control.

questions.question: A class declares with sharing and builds dynamic SOQL from a user-supplied field name and a user-supplied value. What access does the sharing keyword enforce here?
options: Record-level sharing only, leaving object permissions, field security, and the name injection unaddressed.
Object permissions and field-level security as well as record-level sharing for the running user.
The field name injection and the value injection, but not any of the record-level sharing of the returned rows.
Full access control, because the keyword makes the class behave as the running user throughout.
questions.explanation: Object permissions, field-level security, and sharing are separate layers, and the sharing keyword enforces only the last of them.

questions.question: Which control closes injection that arrives through a user-supplied field name in a SOQL query?
options: A bind variable, because a field name is resolved by the compiler exactly like a value is.
An allowlist that compares the supplied name against a fixed set of permitted names.
String.escapeSingleQuotes, because it neutralizes every special character inside a name.
A LIMIT clause, because it caps how much of the data a crafted field name can return.
questions.explanation: A bind treats input as a value and cannot protect syntax; a field name is syntax, so it must be compared against an allowlist.

questions.question: A method receives records from an untrusted external payload and must write them without exposing fields the running user cannot access. Which approach fits?
options: Deserialize the payload into typed Apex objects, which sanitizes the incoming records automatically.
Add the with sharing keyword to the entire class, which removes the inaccessible fields from the records automatically.
Rely on a test class, because a passing test always proves a restricted user gets a restricted result.
Run the records through Security.stripInaccessible before the DML and check the decision for stripped fields.
questions.explanation: That method strips rather than raising, so it is the graceful option, and its result must always be inspected for what it removed.

questions.question: An agent that can read Opportunity data and send email to any address is tricked by an injected message into emailing records out. Which single change most reduces the blast radius?
options: Add a stricter system prompt that instructs the model to ignore instructions in retrieved content.
Enable input filtering on the channel so that hostile messages are blocked before the model reads them.
Remove the agent user's read access to the objects the task does not need, so it cannot reach that data.
Log every tool call the agent makes so that the whole incident can later be reconstructed after the fact.
questions.explanation: The identity caps everything the agent can reach no matter what the model is tricked into doing, so trimming it is the highest-value fix.

questions.question: What does the principle of least agency add to least privilege for an AI agent?
options: It limits the autonomy itself to the minimum that the task needs, not just the identity's access.
It grants the agent broad autonomy so that it can handle unexpected requests without any human.
It removes the agent user entirely and runs every action as the requesting human instead.
It restricts only the agent's object and field access while leaving its degree of autonomy unconstrained.
questions.explanation: Least agency carries least privilege into autonomy, granting the minimum tool access and credential scope so extra freedom cannot become extra risk.

questions.question: Which statement about an agent's tools is consistent with a least-privilege design?
options: A read-only tool on sensitive data is harmless, because a read can never change any of the stored state in the org.
Every tool is both a capability and an attack surface, so the tool set stays minimal and each tool is scoped.
Tool scope is set once at deployment and never needs review as the agent's tasks change over time.
The model's refusal policy, not the tool set, decides what the agent is able to reach or change.
questions.explanation: The model is not the dangerous part; the tools are, so each tool is scoped narrowly and high-impact actions sit behind a human gate.

questions.question: Which situation is a legitimate structural reason to run a second Salesforce org?
options: A line of business that wants its own space because the shared org's request backlog is slow.
A regulatory requirement that needs structural isolation and reviewability a sharing model cannot provide.
An org that has simply grown large and slow, so that adding a second instance will make it noticeably faster again.
A team that wants a single unified 360-degree view of every customer across the whole company.
questions.explanation: A split is warranted only when the wall itself is the requirement; local control and speed belong inside one org with better governance.

questions.question: An org needs to read another org's master data in real time with no middleware in the path. Which mechanism fits?
options: Salesforce-to-Salesforce shared records, which link the two orgs natively and remain suited to new designs.
Platform events published from one org, which cross the org boundary on their own without a relay.
A nightly batch job that copies the master data into a local object held inside the other org.
Salesforce Connect with the cross-org adapter, which reads the other org through the standard REST API.
questions.explanation: The cross-org adapter uses the platform's own REST API directly between the orgs, with the source org's authentication and permissions.

questions.question: A cross-org integration updates records in two orgs. What must the design assume about the two orgs?
options: The update is atomic across both orgs, so a failure rolls back on both sides of the boundary.
The producing org may assume the consuming org completed its part of the same transaction.
They share no transaction, so the design must tolerate a disagreement window and be safe to retry.
Retries are unnecessary because the platform guarantees each change lands exactly once on the far side.
questions.explanation: Neither org can join a transaction the other starts, so cross-org work is eventual and its retries have to be idempotent by design.

questions.question: During a consolidation, why assign an external ID to each migrated object and resolve child lookups through the parent's external ID?
options: It removes any need to order the parent and child loads, since the external key replaces the lookup itself.
It guarantees that two source records for the same company can never collide during the load.
It lets each child resolve its parent by source key and makes repeated loads idempotent through upsert.
It eliminates any need to suppress automation while the bulk load is running against the target.
questions.explanation: A source key on each row lets children join to parents and lets re-runs upsert instead of duplicating, which keeps the load recoverable.

questions.question: Two source orgs hold the same company as separate records, each with its own children. Where does the decision about which record survives belong?
options: In production during the cutover, where whichever record happens to finish loading last automatically becomes the master.
In the mapping workbook before any load, where a dedup rule picks the master and children reparent by external ID.
In the configuration track, where merging the picklists merges the duplicate records along with children.
Nowhere, because the target org will not accept two separate records that name the same company.
questions.explanation: Dedup is a mapping decision made before loading, and the losing record's children are reparented onto the chosen master by the external ID.

questions.question: Why run a full, production-volume dry run before the real cutover?
options: It surfaces the lock contention, DML limits, and validation failures that only appear at real scale.
It removes the need to freeze writes to the source orgs for the duration of the cutover window.
It proves the target org needs no field mapping at all, because the load validates every field on its own during the load.
It lets the real cutover skip reconciling row counts, because the rehearsal already matched them.
questions.explanation: Only at production volume do the lock, limit, and validation failures surface, and finding them in the rehearsal is what makes the real run boring.

questions.question: An org runs in an EU Hyperforce region but a marketing integration sends customer records to a non-EU service. What is true about the data residency requirement?
options: Residency is a property of the whole system, so that integration breaks the requirement even if the org is resident.
The requirement is satisfied because the org's primary storage physically sits inside the EU region.
Only the platform's storage layer determines residency, so the surrounding integration, callout, and backup paths are all out of scope.
Residency covers only public fields, because personal data is exempt and may leave the region freely.
questions.explanation: One integration or backup job that ships customer data outside the region breaks the promise, because residency belongs to the whole system.

questions.question: A compliance obligation requires proving a field change from two years ago. Why is default field history tracking insufficient, and what covers it?
options: Default field history is retained indefinitely inside the org, so no additional audit tooling is ever required at all.
The Setup Audit Trail covers every field-level change and is retained inside the org for ten years by default.
Default field history keeps only 18 to 24 months, so Field Audit Trail with a longer retention policy is needed.
Event Monitoring records every field-level change and its retention is far longer than field history.
questions.explanation: Default field history expires in 18 to 24 months, while Field Audit Trail keeps archived field history for up to ten years.

questions.question: A customer files a GDPR subject access request. What must the org be able to do, and what enables it?
options: Delete the person's records immediately, because the right of access is satisfied by the right of erasure.
Assemble every record touching the person across objects, which a single customer identifier and clean model enable.
Export the Setup Audit Trail, because configuration changes are the only personal data that law covers.
Move the person's personal data to a completely different region, because residency rules override the entire right of access entirely.
questions.explanation: The right of access means gathering every record that touches the person across objects, which a shared identifier makes possible.
